This is not like asking a friend to babysit a child—the stakes are far higher. Caregivers (even friends) should not be put in positions where they feel they’re being asked to perform intimate, degrading tasks. #### **C. Communicate Directly with Her (Not Her Friend)** - Instead of asking her best friend to step in, **talk to your girlfriend** about what you’re feeling. Say something like: > *"I love you, and I want to support you, but I’m at my limit right now. Can we figure out a way to get you the help you need so I can rest without feeling like I’m abandoning you?"* - This opens the door for her to **ask for professional help** (e.g., a crisis line, therapist, or DID specialist) or to **coordinate with her support network** in a way that feels safe for her. #### **B. Explore Professional Respite Care** - Many people with DID have **caregiver burnout** issues. Look into: - **DID-friendly therapists** who can help with crisis management. - **Respite care services** (some mental health organizations offer short-term support). - **Co-hosting** (if she has a trusted friend or therapist who can help during transitions). #### **C. Address Your Own Boundaries** - If you’re struggling to care for her, it’s okay to **set limits**—but do so **collaboratively**. For example: > *"I care about you, but I need to prioritize my own mental health. Can we work together to find a solution that works for both of us?"* - If she reacts poorly, that’s **her issue**, not yours. You’re not obligated to endure unsustainable care without support. #### **D. Educate Yourself on DID** - DID is often misunderstood. Learning more about it (e.g., from [ISST-D](https://www.isst-d.org/), [DID Alliance](https://www.did-alliance.org/), or books like *Trauma and the Multiple Self*) can help you understand her experience better and avoid well-intentioned but harmful actions. --- ### **3. Why This Situation Is So Painful** - **Guilt vs. Self-Care**: You likely feel guilty for "abandoning" her, but **self-preservation is not selfish**—especially when you’re not equipped to handle a week-long crisis alone. - **Stigma Around DID**: Many people (including friends and partners) don’t understand DID, which can lead to **misguided "help"**. Your girlfriend may have felt **exposed or violated** because her best friend was put in an awkward position. - **Power Dynamics**: Even if her best friend agreed, **she (the adult woman) should have been the one to decide** who assists her. Delegating this without her consent can feel like **treating her like a child**—which is the opposite of what DID awareness should promote. --- ### **4. Moving Forward** - **Apologize sincerely** to your girlfriend for how you handled it. Acknowledge that you didn’t respect her autonomy and that you were overwhelmed. Say: > *"I’m sorry I didn’t handle this better. I should have talked to you first instead of asking your friend to step in. I love you, and I want to figure out how to support you without burning out."* - **Work on a care plan together**. This could include: - Identifying **trusted professionals** (therapist, crisis team) she can call in emergencies. - Setting **realistic boundaries** for what you can handle. - Exploring **respite options** (e.g., a friend who knows how to assist without crossing lines). - **Seek therapy for yourself**. If you’re struggling with caregiving, a therapist can help you navigate this without resentment or burnout. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Not Acceptable)** This wasn’t a good solution, even if your intentions were good. **Caregiving should never feel like a chore to be outsourced without consent**, especially when it involves such intimate and vulnerable care. The right approach is **collaboration, communication, and systemic support**—not delegation to someone else in a way that could feel degrading.
